page.title: Deep Dive: The No-JS Static Site with XSLT

headerContent.h1: Deep Dive: The No-JS Static Site with XSLT
headerContent.p: An analysis of the Evidlo/xsl-website repository and the art of building websites with zero JavaScript, no build steps, and no server-side code.

section.p: The Evidlo/xsl-website repository demonstrates a fascinating, minimalist approach to web development: building a static website using only browser-native XSLT (Extensible Stylesheet Language Transformations). The core idea is to completely avoid JavaScript, build tools (like Webpack or Vite), and server-side processing.
Its architecture is elegantly simple, relying on three key components:

ul.li: XML Pages: Raw content and data structured in XML files (e.g., index.xml).
XSL Template: A single XSL file (template.xsl) that defines the HTML structure and transforms the XML content into a viewable page.
CSS Styling: A standard stylesheet (styles.css) to apply visual design to the generated HTML.

section.p: The magic happens directly in the browser. When a user navigates to an .xml file, the browser sees a special processing instruction at the top:

This tells the browser to fetch template.xsl and use it to transform the current XML document into an HTML document. The browser's built-in XSLT processor handles this entire transformation client-side before rendering the page. Once the HTML is generated, the browser applies the linked CSS file as it would for any normal webpage.
The repository also showcases more advanced patterns, such as nested templates and modular content fields, demonstrating that this technique can be used for more than just the most basic sites.

ul.li: No Build Step: Deploy by simply uploading files.
Simple Deployment: Works on any basic web server.
Standard URLs: Clean URLs ending in .xml.
Zero Dependencies: No npm, no frameworks, just the browser.
Manual Indexing: Servers don't list directory contents, so navigation links must be manually maintained.
Partial Browser Support: While widely supported, edge cases and inconsistencies exist.
XSLT 1.0 Only: Browsers are generally stuck on the older XSLT 1.0 standard.
Performance Pitfalls: Complex transformations can be slow on the client side.

section.p: The project sparked interesting discussions on platforms like Hacker News and Reddit, where it was praised for its clever, "retro-modern" simplicity.

blockquote.p: “A funky option for doing client-side includes and basic templating without JS.”

“I love this! It reminds me of the ‘good old days’ of web development, where you could just FTP some files to a server and have a website. No complex build pipelines, no package managers, just simple, elegant files.”

section.p: The author, Evidlo, also clarified a key limitation on Reddit:

blockquote.p: “...not possible to get file lists over HTTP... need manual index.”

section.p: This setup is not a replacement for modern frameworks, but it excels in specific scenarios:

ul.li: Documentation Sites: Where content is structured and changes are infrequent.
Personal Blogs: For developers who value simplicity and full control.
Archival Projects: Creating durable, dependency-free web content.

section.p: Potential Pitfalls: Be mindful of browser quirks, the lack of dynamic capabilities beyond what XSLT offers, and the developer ergonomics, which can feel dated compared to modern static site generators.
Let's build a simple blog using this method. Create the following file structure:

pre.code:
<xsl:value-of select="title"/>
Home First Post

Welcome to my Blog

This is the homepage. Check out my first post!

My First Post

This is the content of my first blog post. Hello, world!

section.p: Upload these files to any static web host, and you have a functioning blog! Remember to update the navigation in template.xsl manually whenever you add a new post.

footerContent.p: A collaborative creation exploring web technologies.
